results.pageText: Staff Platform Engineer Location Remote Employment Type Full time Location Type Remote Department Engineering & Product Compensation $180K – $230K Overview Application About Playlab Playlab is a tech non-profit dedicated to helping educators and students become critical consumers and creators of AI. We believe that an open-source, community-driven approach is key to harnessing the potential of AI in education. We equip educators & students to build custom AI apps for their unique context. Over 100,000 educators have published apps on Playlab. At Playlab, we believe that AI is a new design material, one that should be shaped by many to bring their ideas about learning to life. If you're passionate about building creative, equitable futures for students and teachers, we hope you'll join us. About the role Playlab is looking for a Staff Platform Engineer to build the infrastructure and APIs that let anyone deploy edtech apps that are good and safe for students by default. Every new AI capability, from image generation to agent memory, arrives built for adults and businesses. On Playlab, students and teachers use these capabilities to build their own apps and agents, so each one has to work differently: web search with safety controls a district can tune, memory that doesn't harden into assumptions about a student, storage APIs that understand relationships between people in the school. We're adding capabilities Playlab doesn't have yet and breaking the app we grew up as into composable, reusable building blocks for building the next generation of edtech. Our own engineers build on them first, then teammates who don't write code, then educators and students making apps tailored to their own classrooms. You'll join the platform team we're building to shape what those blocks are and lead the design and implementation of key pieces. We're committed to open sourcing our infrastructure over time, so your design decisions will be used well beyond Playlab. This is a staff level individual contributor role reporting to engineering leadership. You'll stay close to schools and users and work with product, privacy and security, trust and safety, learning engineering, and machine learning to build products and agents on top of your work. What you'll do Build the building blocks Make powerful capabilities right for education. Build capabilities like agent memory, image generation, and data storage with the shape it needs before it reaches a classroom. You'll design these with product, privacy and security, and trust and safety experts, grounded in what we learn in schools, then build them in so every app and agent gets them by default. Design blocks others can build. You'll play a pivotal role in the team deciding how new core infrastructure works - designing APIs and leading builds, so new features and experiences can be scaffolded on solid foundations. Turn our data into something schools can learn from. Grow our warehouse and data vault into the place where schools and their research partners can answer questions about AI in their classrooms. Ship early and learn. You can expect to ship major new infrastructure in production within your first month, and evolve it as new usage patterns emerge. Own where agents run Give educators' agents a powerful place to run. A runtime where the agents and apps educators build can use tools, run code and work for hours on a teacher's behalf, safe enough for classrooms by default. Build the infrastructure for educational evaluations. Make it easy to run, store and compare evaluations at scale that help teachers and students understand where the things they build are performing or not, and help the field learn from what they build. Set the standards and open them up Write the conventions others follow. Create designs and conventions the next several systems are built to and raise the bar for architecture reviews across the team. Build for the commons. Design core infrastructure with a mind towards open sourcing it. How you'll work Start from the classroom. Spend time with teachers, students and our learning engineers to see how a capability will actually be used before you design it. Design with the experts. Work each capability through with product, privacy and security, and trust and safety, and write designs that name the options you rejected, so people can push back early. Prototype, then harden. Get a rough version into real hands quickly, learn from it, and decide which experiments earn a permanent place in the platform. Make the team stronger. Project leadership rotates here. Sometimes you'll lead; often you'll make a teammate's project succeed through design, review and pairing. What the job is really like Mostly building, some operations. Most of your time goes to designing and building blocks, but a real share goes to Terraform, monitoring, alerts and incidents. You won't be shielded from operations. A platform team that's still forming. You'll join a few engineers already on it, plus a devsecops partner and a new security team. It's still small, so you'll do hands-on work a larger company would spread across several teams. Students are on the other end. These systems serve everything from K-12 classrooms to higher ed to ministries of education during the school day. Outages and data mistakes land on teachers and students, so the bar on isolation, privacy and reliability is higher than our size would suggest. You might be a fit if you You're a systems designer who starts from the people using what you build and still loves to ship. You'd rather make ten engineers faster than be the fastest one yourself, and building for students makes a problem more interesting to you, not less. Have designed several systems that worked together as a platform: shared conventions, consistent APIs, and other teams building on them as usage and requirements changed. Have worked with privacy, safety or policy experts to make their requirements part of the product. Have led a few engineers through building new infrastructure: shaped the design with them, broke it into work, got it to production, and left conventions the team kept using. Are hands-on enough with AWS, Kubernetes and Terraform to take what you design to production yourself. Have built systems behind LLM or agent products, and have opinions about what agents need from infrastructure (state, memory, tool access, long-running work). Have built APIs or SDKs that product engineers loved using: clear abstractions, good docs, and a short path from idea to a first working feature. Have changed a design because of what you saw real users do, not just what they asked for. If you meet most of these and the work excites you, we'd love to hear from you. Bonus points for... Building safety or fairness controls into an AI product. Maintaining an open source project other people depend on. Building MCP servers, agent runtimes, sandboxes for untrusted code or LLM gateways, including model routing and cost optimization (we use LiteLLM). Building identity and auth that other products rely on (SSO, OAuth, "sign in with" flows). Building data warehouses or research data pipelines that protect personal data. Working with student or children's data, or in education. Technologies TypeScript, Node, Python, PostgreSQL, AWS (EKS, Bedrock, AgentCore), Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, LiteLLM, NewRelic Why join us? Real impact: Your work shapes how 100,000+ educators around the world use AI with their students, and much of what we build is headed toward the public domain. Real ownership: You'll help decide how the foundations of Playlab's product work, from how agents run to how educators evaluate them, and help lead their release as open source. Room to grow: As Playlab and our platform grow, so does this role, with significant opportunities for learning and growth. Real closeness to users: We're in schools every week (deep-dive 1:1s, group experimentation sessions, strategic planning with entire districts)
